{{short description|Formula for the average value of a function over its domain}}{{More cn|date=January 2023}}

In [[calculus]], and especially [[multivariable calculus]], the '''mean of a function''' is loosely defined as the [[average]] value of the [[function (mathematics)|function]] over its [[domain of a function|domain]]. 

==One-dimensional==
In a [[One dimensional space|one-dimensional domain]], the mean <math>\bar{f}</math> of a function {{math|''f''(''x'')}} over the [[interval (mathematics)|interval]] {{math|[''a'', ''b'']}} is defined by<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dougherty |first1=Bradley |title=On the Average of a Function and the Mean Value Theorem for Integrals |journal=Pi Mu Epsilon Journal |date=2016 |volume=14 |issue=4 |pages=251–254 |jstor=48568127 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/48568127 |access-date=11 January 2023 |issn=0031-952X}}</ref>
<math display="block">
\bar{f}=\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^bf(x)\,dx.
</math>

This definition can be justified as follows.  The average value <math>\bar{y}</math> of finitely many numbers <math>y_1, y_2, \dots, y_n</math> is defined by the property <math>n\bar{y} = y_1 + y_2 + \cdots + y_n</math>. In other words, <math>\bar{y}</math> is the ''constant'' value which when ''added'' <math>n</math> times equals the result of adding the <math>n</math> terms <math>y_1, \dots, y_n</math>. By analogy, a defining property of the average value <math>\bar{f}</math> of a function over the interval <math>[a,b]</math> is that
<math display="block">\int_a^b\bar{f}\,dx = \int_a^bf(x)\,dx .</math>
In other words, <math>\bar{f}</math> is the ''constant'' value which when ''[[integral|integrated]]'' over <math>[a,b]</math> equals the result of integrating <math>f(x)</math> over <math>[a,b]</math>. But the integral of a constant <math>\bar{f}</math> is just
<math display="block">\int_a^b\bar{f}\,dx = \bar{f}x\bigr|_a^b = \bar{f}b - \bar{f}a = (b - a)\bar{f} .</math>

=== Mean value theorem ===
{{main|Mean value theorem}}
The first mean value theorem for integration guarantees that if <math>f</math> is a [[continuous function|continuous]] function on <math>[a,b]</math> then there exists a point <math>c \in (a, b)</math> such that
<math display="block">\int_a^bf(x)\,dx = f(c)(b - a) .</math>
That is, continuous functions have the property that their mean value <math>\bar{f}</math> on a closed interval is actually achieved at some point of the interval: there exists a point <math>c</math> for which <math>\bar{f} = f(c)</math>.

==Multi-dimensional==
In [[multidimensional|several variables]], the mean over a [[relatively compact]] [[domain (mathematical analysis)|domain]] ''U'' in a [[Euclidean space]] is defined by

<math display="block">\bar{f}=\frac{1}{\hbox{Vol}(U)}\int_U f \; dV</math>

where <math>\hbox{Vol}(U)</math> and <math>dV</math> are, respectively, the domain [[volume]] and [[volume element]] (or generalizations thereof, e.g., [[volume form]]).

==Non-arithmetic==
The above generalizes the [[Arithmetic mean|''arithmetic'' mean]] to functions. On the other hand, it is also possible to generalize the [[Geometric mean|''geometric'' mean]] to functions by:

<math display="block">\exp\left(\frac{1}{\hbox{Vol}(U)}\int_U \log f\right).</math>

More generally, in [[measure theory]] and [[probability theory]], either sort of mean plays an important role. In this context, [[Jensen's inequality]] places sharp estimates on the relationship between these two different notions of the mean of a function.

There is also a ''[[harmonic average]]'' of functions and a ''[[quadratic average]]'' (or ''root mean square'') of functions.
